engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Study Plan: 15 Min/Day
chess.body: 15 minutes daily beats 3 hours once a week. Split: 5 min puzzles (Chess.com/Lichess tactics trainer) + 5 min play (1 game, 10+0 or 15+10) + 5 min review (analyse your game, find the turning point). After 30 days: you'll feel patterns automatically. Tactics + play + review = the triangle of improvement.

wisdom.title: Financial Peace = Emotional Peace
wisdom.body: Money stress is the #1 relationship killer. Getting to AED 30K/month isn't just ambition — it's removing a major source of family stress. Every step toward financial stability is a step toward being a calmer, more present parent and partner. The job hunt matters. The income matters. It's not selfish. It's foundational.

book.author: Charlie Munger
book.lesson: Munger's most powerful thinking tool: inversion. Instead of asking 'how do I succeed?' ask 'what would guarantee failure, and how do I avoid that?' The great German mathematician Jacobi said: 'Invert, always invert.' Applied to business: instead of 'how do we grow revenue?' ask 'what is destroying our revenue and how do we eliminate it?' Applied to life: instead of 'how do I be happy?' ask 'what makes people miserable and how do I avoid those things?' Avoiding stupidity is often more important than pursuing brilliance.
book.key_quote: The most reliable path to success is to identify and systematically avoid the most common causes of failure.
book.action: Think of your biggest current goal. List the top 5 things that would guarantee you fail at it. Now focus on eliminating those.
crux: Build a latticework of mental models from many disciplines. One-model thinking distorts every problem.
To the man with a hammer, every problem looks like a nail. Most professionals are that man.
Invert, always invert. Ask how to fail, then avoid that.
Know your circle of competence and stay inside it. The edge is knowing where the edge ends.
Incentives explain most behaviour. Look at the incentive before assuming intent.
The psychology of misjudgement runs about 25 standard biases. Learn them as a checklist.
Opportunity cost is the correct filter for every decision.
Sit on your hands. Great opportunities are rare; act rarely and heavily.
Avoid the three big destroyers: alcohol, leverage, and envy. Envy is the stupidest.
Multiply models: compound interest, scale, backup systems, breakpoints, critical mass.
A great business at a fair price beats a fair business at a great price.
Read constantly. Neither Munger nor Buffett knows a wise person who doesn't read all the time.
Be reliable. Unreliability cancels every virtue you have.
Take a simple idea and take it seriously. That is the whole method.
learnings: Avoiding stupidity beats seeking brilliance, and it is far more achievable.
Inversion surfaces risks that forward thinking never reaches.
Most bad decisions come from one model applied where it doesn't fit.
Patience is a strategy, not a personality trait.
examples: Munger's Costco analysis combines scale economics, incentive design, and psychology at once — no single-discipline read explains it.
See's Candies: Berkshire paid up for brand pricing power in 1972 and it returned over $2bn on a $25m outlay.
Munger rebuilt from a divorce, no money, and the death of his 9-year-old son to become a billionaire. Reliability compounded.
adapt: Invert the Dubai plan: what guarantees no offer by mid-2026? Then remove those causes.
Circle of competence: Indian equities and FP&A. Polymarket stays paper-only until 200 trades say otherwise.
Check incentives before trusting any financial content, including your own.
Sit on your hands when the regime filter says no. Not trading is a position.

minimalism.title: Sentimental ≠ Storage
minimalism.body: You are keeping the object to keep the memory. The memory is not in the object. Photograph it, write one line about why it mattered, and release the thing.
minimalism.action: Photograph one sentimental item you have not looked at in a year.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Thank The Invisible People
etiquette.body: The security guard, the cleaner, the driver, the tea boy. How you treat people who cannot advance your career is the only honest read on your character — and senior people watch for it specifically.
etiquette.action: Learn the name of one person whose name you have never asked.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: The Half-Smile
stillness.body: Thich Nhat Hanh's practice: a slight smile, held, changes state faster than most reasoning about your mood. The body leads the mind more often than the reverse.
stillness.action: Half-smile for one full minute. Notice the shift.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Incentives
model.body: Show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome. Never explain by malice or stupidity what the incentive structure fully predicts. Ask who gets paid for this to happen.
model.action: For one recommendation you received, map who benefits from you following it.
model.label: Mental Model

drill.title: Teach One Thing
drill.body: Explaining to another person exposes every gap instantly. Teaching is the highest-return study method measured, and it costs ten minutes.
drill.action: Teach one concept to someone today. Note where you stumbled.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Grip Strength As A Biomarker
health.body: It correlates with cardiovascular mortality and cognitive decline, and it is trivially measurable. It is a proxy for total-body strength and neuromuscular health.
health.action: Two sets of dead hangs or farmer's carries to failure.
health.label: Health

case.title: Paytm's IPO Disaster
case.story: Paytm IPO at ₹2,150. Fell 27% on listing day. Problem: no clear path to profitability, high cash burn, and no moat in payments. Stock fell 75% from peak.
case.lesson: A business model that relies on subsidized transactions is not a business — it's a bet on market share. Investors eventually ask: where's the profit?

fpna.title: EBITDA Bridge
fpna.body: Walk from prior period: Revenue ±, COGS ±, SG&A ±, Other ±. Bridges tell the story behind the number.

cfo.title: The CA→FC→CFO Timeline
cfo.body: CA qualified → 2-3 years Big 4/audit → Senior FP&A → Finance Manager → Financial Controller (5-8 years post-qualification) → CFO (10-15 years). Dubai compresses this by 2-3 years if you hit the right company at the right growth stage.

money_hack.title: The 50-30-20 Rule
money_hack.body: 50% needs · 30% wants · 20% savings. Automate the 20% on salary day.

dubai.title: The LinkedIn setting that matters most
dubai.body: Set location to Dubai, United Arab Emirates and turn on Open to Work for recruiters only. Gulf recruiters filter by location before they read anything, and a Mumbai location excludes you from the search entirely.
dubai.targets: This is a two-minute change that decides whether you are visible at all.
dubai.action: Location, headline with the target title, and the About section rewritten in numbers.

desk.productivity: Track energy, not just time. Hard work when energy is highest.

father.title: Mirror her expressions
father.do: Copy her face — surprise, frown, smile — and hold it so she sees it.
father.why: Facial mirroring is how infants learn that internal states have external signals. It is the earliest form of emotional literacy.

father.title: Take her outside daily
father.do: Fifteen minutes outdoors, describing what you both see.
father.why: Daylight anchors circadian rhythm, which is the practical route to better night sleep. The narration doubles as vocabulary exposure in a changing environment.

life_wisdom.teaching: Seeing things as they are, before preference distorts them. The first of the three jewels, and deliberately placed before right conduct.
life_wisdom.apply: Separate the number from what you want the number to be. Write the actual result before writing the explanation — the order changes the explanation.

life_wisdom.teaching: The Buddha rejected both indulgence and severe asceticism after trying each. The insight came from testing both, not theorising.
life_wisdom.apply: Applied to risk: neither all-cash nor all-in. Applied to work: neither burnout nor coasting. The middle is a position you have to keep adjusting, not one you find once.

speaking.title: The hostile question
speaking.drill: Rehearse: 'That is a fair challenge — here is the assumption behind it.' Say it five times until it is automatic.
speaking.why: Having a rehearsed opening for a hostile question buys three seconds of thinking without looking rattled.

interview_tech.q: You suspect fraud in a store's cash handling. What is your first move?
interview_tech.a: Do not confront and do not alert. Preserve evidence first — secure the system logs, till data, CCTV and reconciliations before anyone knows there is a question. Then escalate per policy: internal audit, legal, and whoever the fraud policy names, usually the audit committee chair for anything material or involving management. Only then investigate. The most common and most costly mistake is a well-meaning manager asking questions locally, which destroys evidence and tips off the person involved.
interview_tech.who: Any group with an audit committee

interview_tech.q: How would you build the finance case for entering Saudi Arabia?
interview_tech.a: Model it as an option, not a certainty. Entry costs: legal structure and Saudisation obligations under Nitaqat, which drive a materially different payroll cost curve; local content and CITC/ZATCA compliance; e-invoicing (FATOORA) from day one. Revenue: a much larger population than the UAE with different mall economics and a younger consumer. Build the base case on 3–5 stores, not the full ambition, with an explicit go/no-go gate after 24 months and a costed exit. The board decision you want is a staged commitment.

interview_soft.q: What would your last manager say is your weakness?
interview_soft.a: Name a real one with a boundary. The pattern that works: a genuine weakness, evidence you know its cost, and the specific mechanism you use to contain it. 'I go too deep into detail before surfacing a view — it has cost me time on low-stakes analysis. I now set a decision deadline before starting and present at that point regardless of how complete it feels.' Avoid perfectionism, avoid anything that would disqualify you for the role itself.

interview_soft.q: What is the hardest decision you have made in your career?
interview_soft.a: Hard means genuinely two-sided, not merely unpleasant. Redundancies, closing a site, overruling someone you respected, or choosing between two people for one role. Structure: the trade-off, the information you had and did not have, how you decided, what it cost, and what you would do differently. Interviewers discount any answer where the right choice was obvious in hindsight — say what made it genuinely close.
